notebooks.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
notebooks.summary: This revision integrates Renormalization Group (RG) methods and causal graphical frameworks to refine our understanding of memory reliability costs. We find that RG flows suggest universal dissipation bounds are dictated by symmetry-breaking fixed points, while causal graphical hierarchies identify specific edges in the data-generating process where memory must be robust to maintain stability against environment shifts. Furthermore, memory costs in information engines are bounded by the input ensemble's separable-state capacity, extending beyond simple Landauer limits.
notebooks.findings:
The Renormalization Group enables the emergence of symmetries at fixed points, allowing spacetime symmetries to emerge even when broken at intermediate scales, which implies that universal dissipation bounds for memory might be structurally determined by these fixed points. [peer-18fb95596223f27b12685bda]

Memory reliability against environmental shifts is governed by the causal hierarchy of graphical operators, which disable specific edges responsible for dataset shifts; stable memory states must align with these invariants. [peer-29c52687077e3b95ebafdef1]

notebooks.limitations: The integration of high-level renormalization concepts with macroscopic memory retention remains largely theoretical. Empirical data on the energetic cost of maintaining specific invariance classes in non-equilibrium settings is sparse.
notebooks.next_questions: Can we quantify the energy-per-bit cost of maintaining invariance to specific dataset shifts in real-world memory hardware?

detail.title: Thermodynamic and Practical Costs of Memory Reliability
detail.summary: This revision integrates Renormalization Group (RG) methods and causal graphical frameworks to refine our understanding of memory reliability costs. We find that RG flows suggest universal dissipation bounds are dictated by symmetry-breaking fixed points, while causal graphical hierarchies identify specific edges in the data-generating process where memory must be robust to maintain stability against environment shifts. Furthermore, memory costs in information engines are bounded by the input ensemble's separable-state capacity, extending beyond simple Landauer limits.
